summary: Presents a framework for consent-based communications in SIP. SIP lets requests such as invitations and instant messages reach a recipient with no consent, which can be misused for abuse, including amplification and denial of service attacks. The framework lets a recipient grant permission before a relay sends them such requests. It was updated later.

plainLanguage.summary: You would not want strangers to ring your bell nonstop. This sets up a way for a person to say yes, it's okay, before a message service will pass things along to them.

questions: how does sip prevent amplification attacks
what is a sip 470 consent needed response
subtitle: How SIP servers that fan a request out to other people first get those people's permission.

tldr.problem: A SIP server can be told to deliver requests such as INVITE and MESSAGE to a person who never agreed to receive them, which enables spam, amplification and denial of service attacks.
tldr.mechanism: Any relay that translates one URI into others must first send each new recipient a MESSAGE carrying a permission document, and only translates towards that recipient after the recipient grants permission through a SIP PUBLISH or an HTTP GET.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5360 is a Proposed Standard that says all relays MUST implement the framework. It has since been updated by RFC 8217.

facts.label: Grant and deny requests
facts.value: SIP PUBLISH or HTTP GET, empty body

today: RFC 5360 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8217. The original text says all relays that perform translations MUST implement the framework.

sections.title: The Consent Problem in SIP
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) carries requests such as INVITE and MESSAGE from an initiator to a recipient. A recipient can reject a request, but a network of SIP proxy servers will deliver it without the recipient's explicit consent.

That lack of consent can cause amplification and DoS (Denial of Service) attacks. RFC 5360 defines a basic framework that adds consent-based communication to SIP. The problems are described in more detail in a companion requirements document, RFC 4453.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now a stranger can make a message service ring your doorbell even if you never asked. This document adds a rule that the service must ask you first.

sections.title: Relays and Translations
sections.content:
The framework is built around the relay: any SIP server (a proxy, a B2BUA or a hybrid) that receives a request, translates its Request-URI into one or more next-hop URIs, and delivers the request to them. The incoming Request-URI is the target URI. The outgoing ones are recipient URIs.

Translations cause the consent problem in two ways. Translations based on local data, such as registrations, are how a request reaches an endpoint it could not otherwise reach. Translations that produce more than one recipient URI are a source of amplification. Servers that do not translate, such as outbound proxies, do not cause amplification.

The framework lets potential recipients agree to be actual recipients by giving the relay permission to send them traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay is like a mail room that takes one letter and makes copies for several people. The rule is that it may only copy letters for people who said yes.

sections.title: Architecture and Permissions
sections.content:
A relay stores permissions next to its translation logic. A recipient that has not given permission is simply ignored when the relay translates. Permissions last while the context where they were granted is valid, or until revoked. If a recipient is removed from the translation logic, the relay SHOULD delete its permissions, and it is RECOMMENDED that relays ask recipients to refresh permissions periodically. The RFC gives no refresh interval values.

When a client changes the translation logic, for example by adding a recipient with XCAP or a REGISTER, the relay asks the new recipient for permission with a MESSAGE request. If the user is offline, a store-and-forward server can buffer the request. Domains without one can still use the framework, but a request to an offline user then fails and the client is told through the Pending Additions event package of RFC 5362.

All relays MUST implement the framework. User agents are only RECOMMENDED to, so legacy user agents still work as clients and recipients with acceptable functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay keeps a list of who said yes. If you are away, a helper holds the question until you come back.

sections.title: The Permission Document
sections.content:
A permission document describes the translation that needs approval. It holds the identity of the sender, the identity of the original recipient (the target URI), the identity of the final recipient (the recipient URI), and URIs to grant and to deny permission. Relays MUST support SIP and SIPS URIs for granting and denying and MAY support HTTP and HTTPS URIs.

Documents can use wildcards, and the sender field is expected to often contain one. The recipient URI MUST NOT be wildcarded. Where the sender matters, relays MUST authenticate senders. Entities MUST support the format of RFC 5361.

The MESSAGE request also SHOULD carry a human-readable part with the same information, so that a user agent that does not understand permission documents can show it like any instant message, and the person can click the right URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The permission document is a note that says who wants to send what to whom, with a yes link and a no link.

sections.title: The Permission Flow
sections.content:
In the prototypical flow, user A adds sip:B@example.com to a URI-list relay using XCAP. The relay marks that URI as pending, answers HTTP 202, and sends a MESSAGE with a permission document to B. A subscribes to the pending-additions event to follow progress. When B comes online and fetches stored messages, B sends a PUBLISH to the grant URI. The relay then notifies A that the translation logic was updated.

To resist amplification, the framework uses a credit-based mechanism. Users adding recipients must generate bandwidth comparable to what the relay will generate. So relays MUST NOT allow more than one recipient URI per transaction. An XCAP server SHOULD answer a violation with HTTP 409 (Conflict) and a registrar SHOULD answer with a SIP 403.

A recipient can revoke permission at any time by using the deny URI. A relay that sends traffic to a URI that previously consented SHOULD add a Trigger-Consent header field with a target-uri parameter. A recipient who lost the deny URI can PUBLISH to the URI in that header and receive a fresh permission document by MESSAGE.

Registrations are treated as translations too. A third-party registration could bind an attacker's address of record to a victim's contact, so the registrar asks the contact for permission in the same way. A user agent that registers over the same connection it receives traffic on does not need this.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the relay to add a friend. The relay sends the friend a note with a yes link. When the friend clicks yes, the relay tells you it worked.

sections.title: Authenticating the Grant
sections.content:
A recipient grants or denies permission by sending a SIP PUBLISH or an HTTP GET with an empty body to one of the URIs in the document. The relay MUST make sure that request came from the recipient and not an attacker. It has four methods.

  • SIP Identity (RFC 4474): the relay checks that the sender owns the recipient URI; otherwise it SHOULD answer 401 and MUST NOT process the request.
  • P-Asserted-Identity (RFC 3325): only for networks of trusted SIP servers inside one administrative domain.
  • Return routability: the relay places an unguessable URI in the document and treats any request to it as authenticated. It is weaker than SIP Identity but usable on the current Internet. The MESSAGE MUST go to a SIPS URI, the grant and deny URIs MUST be secure (SIPS and HTTPS), and part of each MUST be cryptographically random with at least 32 bits of randomness.
  • SIP digest: only for recipients that share a secret with the relay.

Only return routability can be used with HTTP GET. When a third-party-registered user agent cannot prove ownership of its URI with the other methods, return routability MUST be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay has to be sure the yes really came from you. It can check your ID, or it can give you a secret link that only you could have received.

sections.title: Request-Contained URI Lists and the 470 Response
sections.content:
Some URI-list services take the list of recipients inside the request itself. Such a relay keeps a list of URIs for which it has permission. If a request names a URI without permission, the relay MUST NOT perform the translation and SHOULD return a 470 (Consent Needed) response, with a Permission-Missing header field listing the URIs that lack permission.

A client that receives a 470 uses a manipulation mechanism such as XCAP to add those URIs, and the relay then obtains permission as usual. A 470 without the header means the client must use another mechanism to find the missing URIs.
sections.plainLanguage: If you try to send to someone who has not said yes, the relay says "consent needed" and tells you exactly who is missing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authenticating clients and preventing spam are out of scope, but they do not replace this framework, because they do not stop an authorized client from adding recipients without their consent. A registrar that accepts no third-party registrations would not need to implement it.

Permission documents and Pending Additions information can be sensitive, and attackers may try to alter a document so a client grants something other than what it thinks. Relays are RECOMMENDED to use strong integrity and confidentiality means, with end-to-end S/MIME preferred and hop-by-hop TLS with SIPS URIs as the fallback. Store-and-forward servers MUST be able to deliver encrypted and integrity-protected messages to their user agents.
sections.plainLanguage: The yes-or-no note must not be changed or read by strangers, so it should travel in a sealed envelope.

items.title: SIP Identity
items.text: PUBLISH only. Relay checks the sender owns the recipient URI.

items.title: P-Asserted-Identity
items.text: PUBLISH only. Trusted networks within one administrative domain.

items.title: Return routability
items.text: PUBLISH or HTTP GET. Unguessable URI sent over a secure channel.

items.title: SIP digest
items.text: PUBLISH only. Recipient shares a secret with the relay.
